claim: The Dorsal Organ Cool Cells (DOCCs) of the Drosophila larva are a set of exceptionally thermosensitive neurons critical for larval cool avoidance.
source: The Dorsal Organ Cool Cells (DOCCs) of the Drosophila larva are a set of exceptionally thermosensitive neurons critical for larval cool avoidance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work establishing DOCC function and thermosensitivity.

claim: DOCC cool-sensing is mediated by Ionotropic Receptors IR21a and IR25a.
source: Here, we show that DOCC cool-sensing is mediated by Ionotropic Receptors (IRs), a family of sensory receptors widely studied in invertebrate chemical sensing. We find that two IRs, IR21a and IR25a, are required to mediate DOCC responses to cooling and are required for cool avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the manuscript, supported by genetic, physiological, and behavioral data presented throughout.

claim: IR21a and IR25a are required for cool avoidance behavior.
source: We find that two IRs, IR21a and IR25a, are required to mediate DOCC responses to cooling and are required for cool avoidance behavior.
evidence: Supported by behavioral thermotaxis experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Ectopic expression of IR21a can confer cool-responsiveness in an Ir25a-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, we find that ectopic expression of IR21a can confer cool-responsiveness in an Ir25a-dependent manner, suggesting an instructive role for IR21a in thermosensing.
evidence: Supported by misexpression experiments in Hot Cells shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: IR21a has an instructive role in thermosensing.
source: Furthermore, we find that ectopic expression of IR21a can confer cool-responsiveness in an Ir25a-dependent manner, suggesting an instructive role for IR21a in thermosensing.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of IR21a misexpression to confer cool sensitivity.

claim: IR family receptors can function together to mediate thermosensation of exquisite sensitivity.
source: Together, these data show that IR family receptors can function together to mediate thermosensation of exquisite sensitivity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental data presented.

claim: The DOCCs robustly respond to decreases in temperature as small as a few millidegrees C per second.
source: The DOCCs robustly respond to decreases in temperature as small as a few millidegrees C per second (Klein et al., 2015), a thermosensitivity similar to that of the rattlesnake pit organ (Goris, 2011), a structure known for its extraordinary sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Klein et al., 2015.

claim: DOCC thermosensitivity is similar to that of the rattlesnake pit organ.
source: The DOCCs robustly respond to decreases in temperature as small as a few millidegrees C per second (Klein et al., 2015), a thermosensitivity similar to that of the rattlesnake pit organ (Goris, 2011), a structure known for its extraordinary sensitivity.
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to Klein et al., 2015 and Goris, 2011.

claim: The rattlesnake pit organ is known for its extraordinary sensitivity.
source: The DOCCs robustly respond to decreases in temperature as small as a few millidegrees C per second (Klein et al., 2015), a thermosensitivity similar to that of the rattlesnake pit organ (Goris, 2011), a structure known for its extraordinary sensitivity.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge cited from Goris, 2011.

claim: The DOCCs are critical for mediating larval avoidance of temperatures below ~20˚C.
source: A combination of laser ablation, calcium imaging and cell-specific inhibition studies was used to establish the DOCCs as critical for mediating larval avoidance of temperatures below ~20˚C, with the thermosensitivity of this avoidance behavior paralleling the thermosensitivity of DOCC physiology (Klein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Klein et al., 2015.

claim: The thermosensitivity of larval cool avoidance behavior parallels the thermosensitivity of DOCC physiology.
source: A combination of laser ablation, calcium imaging and cell-specific inhibition studies was used to establish the DOCCs as critical for mediating larval avoidance of temperatures below ~20˚C, with the thermosensitivity of this avoidance behavior paralleling the thermosensitivity of DOCC physiology (Klein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Klein et al., 2015.

claim: The molecular mechanisms that underlie DOCC thermosensitivity are unknown.
source: While the DOCCs are exceptionally responsive to temperature, the molecular mechanisms that underlie their thermosensitivity are unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Several classes of transmembrane receptors have been shown to participate in thermosensation in animals.
source: At the molecular level, several classes of transmembrane receptors have been shown to participate in thermosensation in animals.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: The most extensively studied thermosensory receptors are the highly thermosensitive members of the Transient Receptor Potential (TRP) family of cation channels.
source: The most extensively studied are the highly thermosensitive members of the Transient Receptor Potential (TRP) family of cation channels (Palkar et al., 2015; Vriens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TRP channels function as temperature-activated ion channels.
source: These TRPs function as temperature-activated ion channels and mediate many aspects of thermosensing from fruit flies to humans (Barbagallo and Garrity, 2015; Palkar et al., 2015; Vriens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TRP channels mediate many aspects of thermosensing from fruit flies to humans.
source: These TRPs function as temperature-activated ion channels and mediate many aspects of thermosensing from fruit flies to humans (Barbagallo and Garrity, 2015; Palkar et al., 2015; Vriens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Anoctamin 1 is a thermosensitive calcium-activated chloride channel that contributes to thermosensation in vertebrates.
source: In addition to TRPs, other classes of channels contribute to thermosensation in vertebrates, including the thermosensitive calcium-activated chloride channel Anoctamin 1 (Cho et al., 2012) and the two pore domain potassium channel TREK-1 (Alloui et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Cho et al., 2012.

claim: TREK-1 is a two pore domain potassium channel that contributes to thermosensation in vertebrates.
source: In addition to TRPs, other classes of channels contribute to thermosensation in vertebrates, including the thermosensitive calcium-activated chloride channel Anoctamin 1 (Cho et al., 2012) and the two pore domain potassium channel TREK-1 (Alloui et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Alloui et al., 2006.

claim: Sensory receptors normally associated with chemical sensing can make important contributions to thermotransduction in Drosophila.
source: Recent work in Drosophila has demonstrated that sensory receptors normally associated with other modalities, such as chemical sensing, can also make important contributions to thermotransduction.
evidence: This is established by recent scientific work.

claim: GR28B(D) is a member of the invertebrate gustatory receptor (GR) family that functions as a warmth receptor.
source: In particular, GR28B(D), a member of the invertebrate gustatory receptor (GR) family, was shown to function as a warmth receptor to mediate warmth avoidance in adult flies exposed to a steep thermal gradient (Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ni et al., 2013.

claim: GR28B(D) mediates warmth avoidance in adult flies exposed to a steep thermal gradient.
source: In particular, GR28B(D), a member of the invertebrate gustatory receptor (GR) family, was shown to function as a warmth receptor to mediate warmth avoidance in adult flies exposed to a steep thermal gradient (Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ni et al., 2013.

claim: Rhodopsin has been reported to contribute to temperature responses.
source: The photoreceptor Rhodopsin has also been reported to contribute to temperature responses, although its role in thermosensory neurons is unexamined (Shen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shen et al., 2011.

claim: The role of Rhodopsin in thermosensory neurons is unexamined.
source: The photoreceptor Rhodopsin has also been reported to contribute to temperature responses, although its role in thermosensory neurons is unexamined (Shen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Ionotropic Receptors (IRs) are a family of invertebrate receptors that have been widely studied in insect chemosensation.
source: Ionotropic Receptors (IRs) are a family of invertebrate receptors that have been widely studied in insect chemosensation, frequently serving as receptors for diverse acids and amines (Benton et al., 2009; Silbering et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IRs frequently serve as receptors for diverse acids and amines.
source: Ionotropic Receptors (IRs) are a family of invertebrate receptors that have been widely studied in insect chemosensation, frequently serving as receptors for diverse acids and amines (Benton et al., 2009; Silbering et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IRs belong to the ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) family.
source: The IRs belong to the ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) family, an evolutionarily conserved family of heterotetrameric cation channels that includes critical regulators of synaptic transmission like the NMDA and AMPA receptors (Croset et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Croset et al., 2010.

claim: The iGluR family is an evolutionarily conserved family of heterotetrameric cation channels.
source: The IRs belong to the ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) family, an evolutionarily conserved family of heterotetrameric cation channels that includes critical regulators of synaptic transmission like the NMDA and AMPA receptors (Croset et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Croset et al., 2010.

claim: The iGluR family includes critical regulators of synaptic transmission like the NMDA and AMPA receptors.
source: The IRs belong to the ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) family, an evolutionarily conserved family of heterotetrameric cation channels that includes critical regulators of synaptic transmission like the NMDA and AMPA receptors (Croset et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Croset et al., 2010.

claim: IRs have been found only in Protostomia.
source: In contrast to iGluRs, IRs have been found only in Protostomia and are implicated in sensory transduction rather than synaptic transmission (Rytz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Rytz et al., 2013.

claim: IRs are implicated in sensory transduction rather than synaptic transmission.
source: In contrast to iGluRs, IRs have been found only in Protostomia and are implicated in sensory transduction rather than synaptic transmission (Rytz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Rytz et al., 2013.

claim: The IR family has undergone significant expansion and diversification in insects.
source: In insects, the IR family has undergone significant expansion and diversification, with the fruit fly D. melanogaster genome encoding 66 IRs (Croset et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Croset et al., 2010.

claim: The fruit fly D. melanogaster genome encodes 66 IRs.
source: In insects, the IR family has undergone significant expansion and diversification, with the fruit fly D. melanogaster genome encoding 66 IRs (Croset et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Croset et al., 2010.

claim: At least some IRs are thought to form heteromeric channels in which a broadly-expressed IR 'co-receptor' partners one or more selectively-expressed 'stimulus-specific' IRs.
source: While the detailed structures of IR complexes are unknown, at least some IRs are thought to form heteromeric channels in which a broadly-expressed IR 'co-receptor' (such as IR25a, IR8a or IR76b) partners one or more selectively-expressed 'stimulus-specific' IRs (Abuin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Abuin et al., 2011.

claim: IR25a, IR8a and IR76b are examples of broadly-expressed IR 'co-receptors'.
source: While the detailed structures of IR complexes are unknown, at least some IRs are thought to form heteromeric channels in which a broadly-expressed IR 'co-receptor' (such as IR25a, IR8a or IR76b) partners one or more selectively-expressed 'stimulus-specific' IRs (Abuin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Abuin et al., 2011.

claim: IR25a is the most highly conserved IR across insect species.
source: Among insect IRs, IR25a is the most highly conserved across species (Croset et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Croset et al., 2010.

claim: IR25a expression has been observed in multiple classes of chemosensory neurons with diverse chemical specificities in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, IR25a expression has been observed in multiple classes of chemosensory neurons with diverse chemical specificities, and IR25a has been shown to function as a 'co-receptor' that forms chemoreceptors of diverse specificities in combination with other, stimulus-specific IRs (Abuin et al., 2011; Rytz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IR25a functions as a 'co-receptor' that forms chemoreceptors of diverse specificities in combination with other, stimulus-specific IRs.
source: In Drosophila, IR25a expression has been observed in multiple classes of chemosensory neurons with diverse chemical specificities, and IR25a has been shown to function as a 'co-receptor' that forms chemoreceptors of diverse specificities in combination with other, stimulus-specific IRs (Abuin et al., 2011; Rytz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IR21a is conserved in mosquitoes and other insects.
source: IR21a is conserved in mosquitoes and other insects, but has not been associated with a specific chemoreceptor function (Silbering et al., 2011), raising the possibility that it may contribute to other sensory modalities.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Silbering et al., 2011.

claim: IR21a has not been associated with a specific chemoreceptor function.
source: IR21a is conserved in mosquitoes and other insects, but has not been associated with a specific chemoreceptor function (Silbering et al., 2011), raising the possibility that it may contribute to other sensory modalities.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Silbering et al., 2011.

claim: Ir21a-Gal4 drives robust gene expression in a subset of neurons in the dorsal organ ganglion.
source: Examining a range of potential sensory receptors in the larva, we found that regulatory sequences from the Ionotropic Receptor Ir21a drove robust gene expression (via the Gal4/UAS system [Brand and Perrimon, 1993]) in a subset of neurons in the dorsal organ ganglion, as well as in other locations (Figure 1b,c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ir21a-Gal4 drives gene expression in three neurons within each dorsal organ ganglion.
source: Within each dorsal organ ganglion, Ir21a-Gal4 drove gene expression in three neurons (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The three Ir21a-Gal4-expressing neurons in each dorsal organ ganglion exhibit the characteristic morphology of the DOCCs.
source: These neurons exhibited the characteristic morphology of the DOCCs, which have unusual sensory processes that form a characteristic 'dendritic bulb' inside the larva (Klein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and citation to Klein et al., 2015.

claim: DOCCs have unusual sensory processes that form a characteristic 'dendritic bulb' inside the larva.
source: These neurons exhibited the characteristic morphology of the DOCCs, which have unusual sensory processes that form a characteristic 'dendritic bulb' inside the larva (Klein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established by citation to Klein et al., 2015.

claim: Ir21a-Gal4-positive neurons are cool-responsive.
source: To confirm that the Ir21a-Gal4-positive neurons were indeed cool-responsive, their thermosensitivity was tested by cell-specific expression of the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6m under Ir21a-Gal4 control.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1d,e.

claim: When exposed to a sinusoidal temperature stimulus between ~14˚C and ~20˚C, GCaMP6m fluorescence in Ir21a-Gal4-positive neurons increased upon cooling and decreased upon warming.
source: Consistent with previously characterized DOCC responses (Klein et al., 2015), when exposed to a sinusoidal temperature stimulus between ~14˚C and ~20˚C, GCaMP6m fluorescence in these neurons increased upon cooling and decreased upon warming (Figure 1d,e and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ir21a-Gal4 and R11F02-Gal4 precisely overlap in three cool-responsive neurons with DOCC morphology in the dorsal organ.
source: As expected, GCaMP6m expressed under the combined control of Ir21a-Gal4 and R11F02-Gal4 revealed their precise overlap in three cool-responsive neurons with DOCC morphology in the dorsal organ, further confirming the identification of the Ir21a-Gal4-expressing cells as the cool-responsive DOCCs (Figure 1f,g).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1f,g.

claim: Ir21a∆1 deletes approximately 11 kb removing all except the last 192 nucleotides of the Ir21a open reading frame.
source: Ir21a∆1 is an ~11 kb deletion removing all except the last 192 nucleotides of the Ir21a open reading frame, including all transmembrane and ion pore sequences (Figure 2a).
evidence: This describes the molecular nature of the mutant allele generated.

claim: Ir21a123 deletes 23 nucleotides in the region encoding the first transmembrane domain of IR21a and creates a translational frameshift.
source: Ir21a123 deletes 23 nucleotides in the region encoding the first transmembrane domain of IR21a and creates a translational frameshift (Figure 2a).
evidence: This describes the molecular nature of the mutant allele generated.

claim: Ir21a∆1 null mutants are unable to navigate away from cooler temperatures and toward warmer temperatures on a thermal gradient.
source: When exposed to a thermal gradient of ~0.36˚C/cm, ranging from ~13.5˚C to ~21.5˚C, Ir21a∆1 null mutants as well as Ir21a123/ Ir21a∆1 heterozygotes were unable to navigate away from cooler temperatures and toward warmer temperatures (Figure 2b,c).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Ir21a123/Ir21a∆1 heterozygotes are unable to navigate away from cooler temperatures and toward warmer temperatures on a thermal gradient.
source: When exposed to a thermal gradient of ~0.36˚C/cm, ranging from ~13.5˚C to ~21.5˚C, Ir21a∆1 null mutants as well as Ir21a123/ Ir21a∆1 heterozygotes were unable to navigate away from cooler temperatures and toward warmer temperatures (Figure 2b,c).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The thermotaxis defects of Ir21a mutants can be rescued by expression of a wild-type Ir21a transcript under Ir21a-Gal4 control.
source: These defects could be rescued by expression of a wild-type Ir21a transcript under Ir21a-Gal4 control and by a wild-type Ir21a genomic transgene (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral rescue data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The thermotaxis defects of Ir21a mutants can be rescued by a wild-type Ir21a genomic transgene.
source: These defects could be rescued by expression of a wild-type Ir21a transcript under Ir21a-Gal4 control and by a wild-type Ir21a genomic transgene (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral rescue data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Ir21a has a critical role in larval thermotaxis.
source: Taken together, these results are consistent with a critical role for Ir21a in larval thermotaxis.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutant and rescue data presented.

claim: Animals homozygous for loss-of-function mutations in Ir8a exhibit robust avoidance of cool temperatures.
source: Animals homozygous for loss-of-function mutations in two previously reported IR co-receptors, Ir8a and Ir76b, exhibited robust avoidance of cool temperatures, indicating that these receptors are not essential for this behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Animals homozygous for loss-of-function mutations in Ir76b exhibit robust avoidance of cool temperatures.
source: Animals homozygous for loss-of-function mutations in two previously reported IR co-receptors, Ir8a and Ir76b, exhibited robust avoidance of cool temperatures, indicating that these receptors are not essential for this behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ir8a and Ir76b are not essential for cool avoidance behavior.
source: Animals homozygous for loss-of-function mutations in two previously reported IR co-receptors, Ir8a and Ir76b, exhibited robust avoidance of cool temperatures, indicating that these receptors are not essential for this behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ir25a2 null mutants fail to avoid cool temperatures.
source: By contrast, Ir25a2 null mutants failed to avoid cool temperatures, a defect that could be rescued by the introduction of a transgene containing a wild type copy of Ir25a (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The cool avoidance defect of Ir25a2 null mutants can be rescued by a transgene containing a wild type copy of Ir25a.
source: By contrast, Ir25a2 null mutants failed to avoid cool temperatures, a defect that could be rescued by the introduction of a transgene containing a wild type copy of Ir25a (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral rescue data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Ir25a participates in cool avoidance.
source: Thus, Ir25a also participates in cool avoidance.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutant and rescue data presented.

claim: Robust IR25a protein expression is detected in multiple cells in the dorsal organ ganglion, including the three Ir21a-Gal4-expressing DOCCs.
source: To assess IR25a expression, larvae were stained with antisera for IR25a. Robust IR25a protein expression was detected in multiple cells in the dorsal organ ganglion, including the three Ir21a-Gal4-expressing DOCCs (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Within DOCCs, IR25a strongly labels the 'dendritic bulbs'.
source: Within DOCCs, IR25a strongly labels the 'dendritic bulbs', consistent with a role in sensory transduction.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: IR25a staining is absent in Ir25a null mutants.
source: Staining was absent in Ir25a null mutants demonstrating staining specificity (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Ir25a is required for thermotaxis.
source: Thus Ir25a is required for thermotaxis and is expressed in the neurons that drive this behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from behavioral and expression data.

claim: Ir25a is expressed in the neurons that drive thermotaxis behavior.
source: Thus Ir25a is required for thermotaxis and is expressed in the neurons that drive this behavior.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3.

claim: DOCCs exhibit strongly reduced responses to cooling in Ir21a∆1 deletion mutants.
source: Consistent with a role for Ir21a in cool responses, DOCCs exhibited strongly reduced responses to cooling in Ir21a∆1 deletion mutants, and this defect was robustly rescued by expression of an Ir21a transcript in the DOCCs using R11F02-Gal4 (Figure 4a-e,h).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The reduced DOCC cool responses in Ir21a∆1 mutants are robustly rescued by expression of an Ir21a transcript in the DOCCs using R11F02-Gal4.
source: Consistent with a role for Ir21a in cool responses, DOCCs exhibited strongly reduced responses to cooling in Ir21a∆1 deletion mutants, and this defect was robustly rescued by expression of an Ir21a transcript in the DOCCs using R11F02-Gal4 (Figure 4a-e,h).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging rescue data shown in Figure 4.

claim: DOCC thermosensory responses are greatly reduced in Ir25a mutants.
source: Similarly, DOCC thermosensory responses were greatly reduced in Ir25a mutants, a defect that was rescued by a wild type Ir25a transgene (Figure 4f–h).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The reduced DOCC thermosensory responses in Ir25a mutants are rescued by a wild type Ir25a transgene.
source: Similarly, DOCC thermosensory responses were greatly reduced in Ir25a mutants, a defect that was rescued by a wild type Ir25a transgene (Figure 4f–h).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging rescue data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Ir21a and Ir25a have a critical role in the detection of cooling by the DOCCs.
source: Together these data demonstrate a critical role for Ir21a and Ir25a in the detection of cooling by the DOCCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutant and rescue calcium imaging data.

claim: DOCC responses to cooling appear unaffected in brv1 mutants.
source: Although brv1 mutant showed defects in thermotactic behavior, DOCC responses to cooling appeared unaffected in brv1 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: brv2 nulls exhibit no detectable thermotaxis defects.
source: brv2 nulls exhibited no detectable thermotaxis defects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No role for brv1 and brv2 in cool sensing by the DOCCs is detected.
source: Thus, we detect no role for these receptors in cool sensing by the DOCCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral and calcium imaging data for brv mutants.

claim: Ectopic expression of IR21a in Hot Cell thermoreceptors confers cool-sensitivity.
source: However, ectopic expression of IR21a in one set of neurons in the adult, Hot Cell thermoreceptors in the arista that normally respond to warming rather than cooling, conferred cool-sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Hot Cell thermoreceptors in the arista normally respond to warming rather than cooling.
source: However, ectopic expression of IR21a in one set of neurons in the adult, Hot Cell thermoreceptors in the arista that normally respond to warming rather than cooling, conferred cool-sensitivity.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: Wild-type HC neurons respond to warming with robust increases in intracellular calcium.
source: As previously reported (Gallio et al., 2011), wild-type HC neurons respond to warming with robust increases in intracellular calcium and to cooling with decreases in intracellular calcium, as reflected in temperature-dependent changes in GCaMP6m fluorescence (Figure 5a,c).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5 and citation to Gallio et al., 2011.

claim: Wild-type HC neurons respond to cooling with decreases in intracellular calcium.
source: As previously reported (Gallio et al., 2011), wild-type HC neurons respond to warming with robust increases in intracellular calcium and to cooling with decreases in intracellular calcium, as reflected in temperature-dependent changes in GCaMP6m fluorescence (Figure 5a,c).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5 and citation to Gallio et al., 2011.

claim: HC neurons in which IR21a is expressed under the control of a pan-neuronal promoter frequently exhibit elevations in calcium in response to both warming and cooling.
source: In contrast, HC neurons in which IR21a is expressed under the control of a pan-neuronal promoter (N-syb>Ir21a animals) frequently exhibited elevations in calcium not only in response to warming, but also at the coolest temperatures (Figure 5b,d,f, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ectopic IR21a expression causes HC neurons, which are normally inhibited by cooling, to become responsive to both cooling and warming.
source: Thus, ectopic IR21a expression causes HC neurons, which are normally inhibited by cooling, to become responsive to both cooling and warming.
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Robust IR25a protein expression is observed in the HC neurons.
source: Consistent with previously reported IR25a expression in the arista (Benton et al., 2009), we observed robust IR25a protein expression in the HC neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to Benton et al., 2009.

claim: Ectopic IR21a expression fails to drive significant HC neuron cool responses in Ir25a mutants.
source: Consistent with a role for Ir25a in Ir21a-mediated cool-responsiveness, ectopic IR21a expression failed to drive significant HC neuron cool responses in Ir25a mutants (Figure 5e,f).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: IR21a can confer cool-sensitivity upon an otherwise warmth-responsive neuron in an Ir25a-dependent fashion.
source: Thus, IR21a can confer cool-sensitivity upon an otherwise warmth-responsive neuron in an Ir25a-dependent fashion.
evidence: This is inferred from the misexpression and mutant data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ectopic expression of IR21a in Gr28b mutant HC neurons yields neurons that respond only to cooling.
source: Finally, ectopic expression of IR21a in Gr28b mutant HC neurons, which lack the Gr28b(D) warmth receptor, yields neurons that respond only to cooling (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Gr28b mutant HC neurons lack the Gr28b(D) warmth receptor.
source: Finally, ectopic expression of IR21a in Gr28b mutant HC neurons, which lack the Gr28b(D) warmth receptor, yields neurons that respond only to cooling (Figure 6).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Gr28b mutant.

claim: Ectopic IR21a expression can confer cool-sensitivity in an Ir25a-dependent fashion.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that ectopic IR21a expression can confer cool-sensitivity in an Ir25a-dependent fashion.
evidence: This is inferred from the misexpression experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The ionotropic receptors IR21a and IR25a have critical roles in thermosensation in Drosophila.
source: These data demonstrate that the ionotropic receptors IR21a and IR25a have critical roles in thermosensation in Drosophila, mediating cool detection by the larval dorsal organ cool cells (DOCCs) and the avoidance of cool temperatures.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all experimental data.

claim: IR21a and IR25a mediate cool detection by the larval dorsal organ cool cells (DOCCs).
source: These data demonstrate that the ionotropic receptors IR21a and IR25a have critical roles in thermosensation in Drosophila, mediating cool detection by the larval dorsal organ cool cells (DOCCs) and the avoidance of cool temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in Figures 1, 4.

claim: IR21a and IR25a mediate the avoidance of cool temperatures.
source: These data demonstrate that the ionotropic receptors IR21a and IR25a have critical roles in thermosensation in Drosophila, mediating cool detection by the larval dorsal organ cool cells (DOCCs) and the avoidance of cool temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data in Figure 2.

claim: Combinations of IRs have been previously found to contribute to a wide range of chemosensory responses, including the detection of acids and amines.
source: Combinations of IRs have been previously found to contribute to a wide range of chemosensory responses, including the detection of acids and amines (Rytz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Rytz et al., 2013.

claim: The findings extend the range of sensory stimuli mediated by IR receptor combinations to cool temperatures.
source: These findings extend the range of sensory stimuli mediated by these receptor combinations to cool temperatures.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: IR21a- and IR25a-dependent cool sensation appears independent of Brivido 1 and Brivido 2.
source: Interestingly, IR21a- and IR25a-dependent cool sensation appears independent of Brivido 1 and Brivido 2, two TRP channels implicated in cool sensing in the adult (Gallio et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the brv mutant data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.
